issues.title: Reject non-positive --line-length values instead of silently accepting them
issues.body:
Black accepts --line-length 0 or --line-length -1 without an error. A negative line-length in pyproject.toml is accepted too. It then formats valid code into extremely narrow output and exits successfully.

For example:

total = price * quantity * (1 + tax_rate)

Run:
black --line-length -1 example.py

The result is still valid Python, so this isn't source corruption. But the docs don't describe a meaning for non-positive line lengths. Would it make sense to reject them with a usage error?

I have a patch using click.IntRange(min=1) for the CLI option, which also validates pyproject.toml values, plus regression tests. The programmatic black.Mode API stays unchanged. This follows the input-validation approach in #5211.

issues.title: Setting the 2027 stable style
issues.body:
2026: #4875 Ruff: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/30022 While many of the "controversial" changes may seem like objectively better formatting to some, the current formatting is well established, and stabilizing some of these larger changes would cause a lot of churn for all users. Ordered by most controversial to least:
hug_parens_with_braces_and_square_brackets **Input** ```py func( { "a": 37, "b": 42, "c": 927, } ) ``` **Output (off)** *unchanged* **Output (on)** ```py func({ "a": 37, "b": 42, "c": 927, }) ``` Currently in `--unstable`, but the crash in #4036 has been fixed. We should probably at least move it from unstable to preview. Causes lots of changes across many many lines, but it's always a decrease and generally increases readability. Proposed changes: - #4099 - note this example is currently unchanged from stable style, so we could implement this post-stabilization without churn - #4098 - in some senses, this is asking for the opposite as the previous [diff-shades-run](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34341327/hug_parens_with_braces_and_square_brackets.html)
wrap_long_dict_values_in_parens **Input** ```py { "a key in my dict": a_very_long_variable * and_a_very_long_function_call() / 100000.0, "another key": (short_value), } ``` **Output (off)** *unchanged* **Output (on)** ```py { "a key in my dict": ( a_very_long_variable * and_a_very_long_function_call() / 100000.0 ), "another key": short_value, } ``` Could cause a lot of churn. Adds more parentheses and sometimes more lines to reduce line length. Defered for many years (since 2023). Ruff has decided this is a non-goal (astral-sh/ruff#12856, #4123). Most of the negative feedback from the past few years (#4882 covers much of it) is fixed by the currently unmerged #5627 - for expressions like single names or strings, parens are retained as-written. [diff-shades-run](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34341321/wrap_long_dict_values_in_parens.html)
split_implicit_string_concatenations_at_newlines **Input** ```py ValueError( "Invalid input:\n" f" * x={x}\n" f" * y={y}\n" f" * z={z}" ) a = ( "

" '

\n' "

" '

\n' '
\n" ) ``` **Output (off)** *unchanged* **Output (on)** ```py ValueError("Invalid input:\n" f" * x={x}\n" f" * y={y}\n" f" * z={z}") a = ( "

" '

\n' "

" '

\n' '
\n" ) ``` I think this is a good change. In many cases it's more inconsistent (i.e the second example is broken after some strings but not others), but I think it may encourage people to manually join/split strings at `\n`, which makes them much more readable. Obviously the ideal solution would be #1467 but that's its own can of worms. [diff-shades-run](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34343369/split_implicit_string_concatenations_at_newlines.html)
wrap_comprehension_in **Input** ```py result = [ very_very_very_very_very_long_item for very_very_very_very_very_long_item in some_very_very_very_very_very_very_long_function_name ] filtered_trait_instructions: list[str] = [ trait for trait in (traits_instructions or []) if trait ] filtered_trait_instructions: list[str] = [ trait for trait in traits_instructions or [] if trait ] ``` **Output (off)** *unchanged* **Output (on)** ```py result = [ very_very_very_very_very_long_item for very_very_very_very_very_long_item in ( some_very_very_very_very_very_very_long_function_name ) ] filtered_trait_instructions: list[str] = [ trait for trait in (traits_instructions or []) if trait ] filtered_trait_instructions: list[str] = [ trait for trait in traits_instructions or [] if trait ] ``` Black currently doesn't add or remove parentheses here at all, so this change tries to standardize them. Black now auto-wraps these clauses if it allows it to fit within the line length, and also prefers wrapping clauses rather than splitting within them. Changed after last year's feedback to retain the written parentheses if it wouldn't be broken across multiple lines. That also heavily decreased the scope of the change. [diff-shades-run](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34341334/wrap_comprehension_in.html)
symmetric_collection_operations **Input** ```py names = ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "Diana", "Edward"] + [ "Fiona", "George", "Harriet", "Isabelle", ] ``` **Output (off)** *unchanged* **Output (on)** ```py names = ( ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "Diana", "Edward"] + ["Fiona", "George", "Harriet", "Isabelle"] ) ``` Applies with any operation between any collections with the goal of visual symmetry. Has a narrow scope and clearly improves aesthetics, but I could also see it going either way with the community. Depending on the reception to this change, we may consider #3629/#4455 which expand this style to other formats. However, it's unlikely due to the large scope of those changes, unlike this one, which is very localized. See those issues and their associated PRs for more details. The `%` change was an unintentended but also generally improves readability as well. If anything I could see the `%` change being controversial and may need to be moved into its own style. [diff-shades-run](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34341315/keep_dict_keys_with_operators.html)
pyi_overload_group_blank_lines **Input** ```py @overload def foo(): ... @overload def foo(): ... @overload def foo(): ... @overload def bar(): ... @overload def bar(): ... @overload def baz(): ... ``` **Output (off)** *unchanged* **Output (on)** ```py @overload def foo(): ... @overload def foo(): ... @overload def foo(): ... @overload def bar(): ... @overload def bar(): ... @overload def baz(): ... ``` Seems like an objectively good change to me. issues.title: Odd behavior from `black` when handling long `lambda` functions
issues.body:
<!--
Please make sure that the bug is not already fixed either in newer versions or the
current development version. To confirm this, you have three options:

1. Update Black's version if a newer release exists: `pip install -U black`
2. Install the latest `main` branch directly:
   `pip install "black @ git+https://github.com/psf/black.git"`
3. Or run _Black_ from source on your machine:
   - create a new virtualenv (make sure it's the same Python version);
   - clone this repository;
   - run `pip install -e .[d]`;
   - run `pip install --group tests`
   - make sure it's sane by running `python -m pytest -n auto`; and
   - run `black` like you did last time.
-->

**Describe the bug**

We were doing some work on one of our interfaces on Pyomo, and we noticed a very long line in one of the files. It's a particularly complicated `lambda` line, and we suspect that `black` is not correctly handling it: https://github.com/Pyomo/pyomo/blob/main/pyomo/solvers/plugins/solvers/xpress_direct.py#L225

**To Reproduce**

We are currently using the most recent version of `black`. If you have a line such as:
```python
# test.py
XpressDirect._addCols = lambda self, prob, objx, mstart, mrwind, dmatval, bdl, bdu, names, types: prob.addcols(objx, mstart, mrwind, dmatval, bdl, bdu, names, types)
```

And you run `black` on it, no extra options:
```bash
$ black test.py
```

You get:
```python
XpressDirect._addCols = lambda self, prob, objx, mstart, mrwind, dmatval, bdl, bdu, names, types: prob.addcols(
    objx, mstart, mrwind, dmatval, bdl, bdu, names, types
)
```

The resulting first line is 112 characters long, which is well above the 88 characters default. This might be expected, maybe not, but it looked odd to us.

**Expected behavior**

`black` should make sure each line does, in fact, use the built-in line limit of 88 chars (unless otherwise requested by the user).

**Environment**

<!-- Please complete the following information: -->

- Black's version: black, 26.10.1 (compiled: yes)
- OS and Python version: MacOS, 3.13.18 (but also occurs on Windows)

**Additional context**

Again, this may be expected behavior, so feel free to close if so. We just wanted to be good stewards and report it!

comments.author: shashb27
comments.body:
Reproduced this on current main (81687b58) — same output, first line is 111 characters. For what it's worth, the same line is still live in pyomo's main today (`pyomo/solvers/plugins/solvers/xpress_direct.py`, line 232) and it's the only over-length line in that file.

I traced where it comes from. Black's splitter only breaks lines at brackets or at delimiters registered at bracket depth 0, and lambda parameter commas are excluded on both counts: `BracketTracker.maybe_increment_lambda_arguments` in `src/black/brackets.py` raises an artificial depth for everything between `lambda` and `:`, and `is_split_after_delimiter` gives those commas priority 0 as a backstop. Python 3 doesn't allow parentheses around lambda parameters, so a long signature has no split point at all. On an assignment black actually does consider wrapping the RHS in parentheses and splitting the body call inside them (the FORCE_OPTIONAL_PARENTHESES second opinion in `run_transformer`), but with this signature the lambda line would still be 91 characters, so it falls back to splitting the call without the parens and leaves the 111-character head. That's also why the same lambda keeps its parens after `return` or as a dict value — the paren-wrapped form only wins when every resulting line fits.

So this looks like the same limitation as #809 rather than a regression, and the fix is really a style decision. The options I see:

- explode the lambda parameters when the lambda is inside brackets (black can add the parens itself on an assignment RHS). This is the only one that actually gets every line under the limit, e.g.:

```python
XpressDirect._addCols = (
    lambda self,
    prob,
    objx,
    mstart,
    mrwind,
    dmatval,
    bdl,
    bdu,
    names,
    types: prob.addcols(objx, mstart, mrwind, dmatval, bdl, bdu, names, types)
)
```

It means touching the lambda-depth machinery and the comment handling around lambda parameters (#5596 and #4640 were both in this area), and the exact shape is what #809 has been debating — but it's doable, and it's the direction @MichaReiser leaned toward there.
- prefer keeping the optional parens around a lambda RHS when the no-paren split leaves a line over-length (small change in `_prefer_split_rhs_oop_over_rhs`). This would make assignments consistent with the `return`/dict-value cases, but the lambda line still exceeds the limit, so it doesn't address the actual report.
- document it as expected behavior and point people at #809; the docs only promise best-effort around one expression per line anyway.

Happy to work on whichever direction sounds right. If this is just a dup of #809, closing this one is fine too — hopefully the trace above is useful either way.

comments.author: MichaReiser
comments.body:
We've since changed the formatting in Ruff. This particular lambda gets formatted to:

```py

    lambda self, prob, objx, mstart, mrwind, dmatval, bdl, bdu, names, types: (
        prob.addcols(objx, mstart, mrwind, dmatval, bdl, bdu, names, types)
```

comments.author: shashb27
comments.body: Verified with ruff 0.17.4 on the same repro — every line fits, the signature line is 79 characters. Interesting detail: black's own second opinion (`FORCE_OPTIONAL_PARENTHESSES` in `run_transformer`) computes 91 characters for its paren-wrapped attempt on the same construct, so there's a measurable gap between the two somewhere in how the wrapped form gets laid out. If black wants parity with Ruff for this case, that delta seems worth understanding — happy to dig into where it comes from.

issues.title: Project-relative cache-dir allows unrestricted pickle.load of attacker-controlled data
issues.body:
### Summary

Black resolves a relative `cache-dir` from `[tool.black]` inside the project checkout and then calls `pickle.load()` on files under that path. Both the metadata cache and the grammar caches are affected.

A repo author can drop crafted pickle files with the expected names. If someone later runs Black on that checkout with caching enabled, the process deserializes them.

This was also shared with Tidelift security, who confirmed the tracing. It was treated as a hardening issue rather than a CVE, which matches Black not claiming untrusted-checkout safety.

### Affected code

- `src/black/files.py` — finds the project `pyproject.toml`
- `src/black/__init__.py` — accepts a relative `cache-dir` from project config and passes it into grammar init (unless `--no-cache`)
- `src/black/cache.py` — metadata cache does unrestricted `pickle.load`
- `src/blib2to3/pgen2/driver.py` + `grammar.py` — grammar cache uses a predictable filename + mtime check, then `pickle.load`

### Preconditions

- Project sets a relative `cache-dir`
- Matching cache files exist for the Black version/mode/Python runtime
- Someone runs Black on the checkout with caching enabled
- `--no-cache` is not used

Cloning alone is not enough.

### Impact

Arbitrary Python code can run as the Black process. Likelihood is limited because the victim has to actually run Black with caching on, and the attacker needs the right filenames.

`--no-cache` blocks both paths.

### Suggested remediation

- Don’t accept `cache-dir` from project config (or only accept absolute paths from a trusted source)
- Switch both caches to a non-executable format, or check that the writer is the same authority as the Black process
- Treat existing project-relative pickle caches as invalid
- Keep an explicit CLI cache dir and `--no-cache` working

Static tracing only. Default cache is still per-user when there’s no project override.

issues.title: Compatible-release requires-python constraints infer unsupported targets
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**

Target-version inference widens a compatible-release constraint when it removes the patch component. `requires-python = "~=3.11.0"` permits Python 3.11 releases, but Black infers Python 3.11 through 3.15 on current `main`.

**To Reproduce**

Create `pyproject.toml`:

```toml
[project]
requires-python = "~=3.11.0"
```

Run:

```sh
black --verbose --config pyproject.toml --code 'x=1'
```

The verbose configuration includes:

```text
target_version: ['py311', 'py312', 'py313', 'py314', 'py315']
```

This can also be reproduced without formatting a file:

```python
from black.files import infer_target_version

print([v.name for v in infer_target_version(
    {"project": {"requires-python": "~=3.11.0"}}
)])
# ['PY311', 'PY312', 'PY313', 'PY314', 'PY315']
```

**Expected behavior**

Only `py311` should be inferred. The [compatible-release specification](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/version-specifiers/#compatible-release) preserves the prefix before the final release component: `~=3.11.0` is equivalent to `>=3.11.0, ==3.11.*`. In contrast, `~=3.11` permits later Python 3 minor versions.

**Environment**

- Black: source checkout of `main`, commit `994ef7eeb18172178552daa1f36f001d156ad583`, installed editable in a clean virtual environment.
- CPython 3.14.6, macOS arm64.
- `packaging` 26.3.

**Additional context**

`strip_specifier_set` turns `~=3.11.0` into `~=3.11`, which loses the upper bound. `~=3.11.7` has the same problem. A focused fix can preserve the matching minor-version prefix while retaining the existing treatment of two-component constraints.

Related: #3581 discusses the strict-`>` lower-bound case; the broader rewrite in #3583 is closed. This report isolates the compatible-release upper-bound case. I have a small patch with regression coverage for patch releases, prereleases, additional release components, exclusions, and the distinct two-component form.

AI assistance: OpenAI Codex helped prepare the reproduction, patch, tests, and report. The outputs above were verified by execution locally.

issues.title: Nested .gitignore negations can never re-include what an ancestor excluded
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**

A negation in a nested `.gitignore` can never re-include something an ancestor `.gitignore`
excluded. Git decides the other way round: the *deepest* gitignore file that has a matching
pattern wins, and only inside that file does last-match-win. Black ORs across gitignore files, so
the deepest one — the only one that can say `!` — is often never consulted.

Effect: `black .` silently skips files that git tracks, and `black --check` passes in CI without a
word about it. rc=0, no warning, no diff.

**To Reproduce**

```
.gitignore                                  ->  .vscode
packages/.gitignore                         ->  !playground/.vscode
packages/playground/.vscode/settings.py
packages/playground/keep.py                 (control)
```

```console
$ git --version
git version 2.55.0
$ git init -q && git add . --dry-run
add '.gitignore'
add 'packages/.gitignore'
add 'packages/playground/.vscode/settings.py'
add 'packages/playground/keep.py'

$ black --check -v .
Identified `/tmp/x` as project root containing a .git directory.
Found input source directory: "/tmp/x"
/tmp/x/.git ignored: matches the --exclude regular expression
/tmp/x/packages/playground/.vscode ignored: matches a .gitignore file content
/tmp/x/packages/playground/keep.py already well formatted, good job.

All done! ✨ 🍰 ✨
1 file would be left unchanged.
```

git tracks `packages/playground/.vscode/settings.py`; Black prunes the directory and never sees
it. `keep.py` is the control — neither tool ignores it, so the fixture isn't just ignoring
everything.

**Cause**

`src/black/files.py`, `_path_is_ignored`:

```python
for gitignore_path, pattern in gitignore_dict.items():
    relative_path = ...
    if pattern.match_file(relative_path):
        return True
return False
```

The dict is ordered least-specific → most-specific (the comment above it says so), and the loop
returns `True` on the *first* match. So an exclusion at the root short-circuits before the nested
file gets a vote. By construction no nested negation can ever undo an ancestor's exclusion.

This is not `pathspec`'s doing. I checked: fed the rules of the file that git says decides, plus
the path relative to *that* directory, `pathspec` answers exactly like git on all of these cases,
in both directions. The divergence lives in the combination layer here.

That matters because #5306 mentions this same divergence in passing and guesses it "likely belongs
in pathspec/traversal upstream". As far as I can measure, it doesn't — it's these lines.

**How often it bites**

I ran Black 26.5.1 against `git check-ignore` over 4,373 queries built from the real `.gitignore`
trees of 43 popular repos. Nine divergences. Eight of them are this bug, in five repos —
`facebook/react` (`packages/.gitignore` with `!playground/.vscode`), `python/cpython`
(`Platforms/Android/testbed/.gitignore` with `!.idea/`), `supabase/supabase`
(`docker/.gitignore` with `!volumes/functions/deno.json*`), and two more. The ninth is a
`pathspec` bug I reported separately (cpburnz/python-pathspec#134).

So it's rare per-query but concentrated: the projects that use nested `.gitignore` negations hit
it every time, and they never find out, because the failure mode is silence.

**A note on the fix**

It is *not* "reverse the iteration order" — that would break the ordinary case where the root
ignores and the nested file says nothing. The rule git implements is: for a given path, find the
deepest gitignore file with any pattern matching it, and let that file's last matching pattern
decide; files closer to the root only get asked if no deeper one matched. Directory pruning during
the walk has to follow the same rule, or the directory disappears before the deeper file is read.
That's more than a four-line change, which is probably why #3694 has been open a while.

Happy to send a PR with the fixture above as a regression test if you'd like it — say the word and
I'll do it against `main`. Not opening one unprompted; I saw the note on #5361.

**Environment**

- Black's version: 26.5.1
- OS and Python version: Linux / Python 3.14.7
- git 2.55.0

comments.author: wahajahmed010
comments.body:
Confirming this is a real divergence from git's precedence rules, and the fix is mostly *not* in `find_project_root` — it's in how black combines ignore patterns across `.gitignore` files.

A quick recap of what git actually does, because the current comment thread hasn't pinned it down yet and it's load-bearing for the fix:

1. For each path, git walks the directory tree from the repo root down and collects *every* matching pattern from every `.gitignore` file along the way.
2. The *last* matching pattern wins **within a single file** (last-match-wins, `!` re-includes).
3. Across files, git does **not** OR them. It applies the patterns in **directory-walk order** (deepest file consulted last), and a `!` in a deeper file overrides an exclude from a shallower file. This is why `packages/.gitignore: !playground/.vscode` works in your repro: git consults the per-directory `packages/.gitignore` *after* the root one, and the negation wins for anything that matches it.

Black, in `src/black/files.py:get_gitignore`, currently ORs the contents of every gitignore together into one big pattern set and then evaluates each path against the union. That collapses the per-file ordering, which is precisely why the deepest gitignore — the only one that can express a useful negation — is functionally shadowed by an ancestor's exclude.

A clean fix that doesn't require black to re-implement git's matcher is to swap the custom ignore handling for `pathspec.PathSpec` (which is already a transitive dep via several dev/test paths, and is what tools like pre-commit, yamllint, and ruff's own gitignore handling use). `PathSpec` builds a `gitwildmatch` spec per-file and applies them in walk order, which gives you the correct "deepest wins" semantics for free and also handles `**/` correctly without the special-casing black currently does. The migration is roughly: replace `get_gitignore` + the `excluded` predicate with a `PathSpec.from_lines("gitwildmatch", chain(root_gitignore, *nested_gitignores))` evaluated against `path.as_posix()`, ordered by walk depth. Edge cases worth pinning down in the same PR:

- `**` interaction with negations (e.g. `**/foo` + `!bar/**` — git treats these asymmetrically because the negation must match the full relative path).
- A `.gitignore` containing only `!` patterns with no positive match — git treats this as a no-op for that directory; black currently may apply the empty match.
- Symlinks: git evaluates ignore patterns against the *real* path, black evaluates against the input path. Unrelated to this bug but worth a one-line note in the PR description.

Two regression tests that would have caught this and should land with the fix:

- Your existing repro (`.vscode` excluded at root, `!packages/playground/.vscode` at `packages/.gitignore` level), asserting that `packages/playground/.vscode/settings.py` is *not* in the excluded set and gets formatted.
- A negated re-include that points at a *file*, not a directory (`packages/.gitignore: !packages/keep.py` while the root excludes `packages/`), asserting `keep.py` is formatted even though its directory is excluded. This is the case where naive "directory-prune" optimizations get it wrong.

I'd suggest filing this as a follow-up to #5376 rather than trying to land it in the same PR as any other gitignore fix — the precedence change is a behavior change for users who happen to rely on black's current (incorrect) behavior, and it's worth a release note.

comments.author: KaizenShogun
comments.body:
I measured the proposed change before endorsing it, and it doesn't hold up — which is a shame,
because the *rule* your recap states is right even though the code line that implements it isn't.
Numbers rather than opinion, `git check-ignore --no-index` (git 2.55.0) as the oracle throughout.

**Where black actually combines the files.** `get_gitignore` builds one `GitIgnoreSpec` **per
`.gitignore` file**, and `_path_is_ignored` walks that dict shallowest-first, returning `True` on the
first hit. The *effect* is an OR, so that part of your description is fair — but the mechanism matters
here, because each spec is already anchored to its own directory. Nothing needs collapsing or
migrating. The only wrong thing is which file gets to decide.

**`PathSpec.from_lines("gitwildmatch", chain(root, *nested))` is that union, and it is worse than
what's there now.** `PathSpec` has no notion of files, directories or walk order — it's a flat pattern
list, so chaining the lines reads every nested pattern as if it lived at the root. On this issue's own
repro, `!playground/.vscode` from `packages/.gitignore` then means `<root>/playground/.vscode`, and the
bug survives untouched. Over 500 randomly generated nested-gitignore trees (4,938 queries):

| rule | agrees with git |
|---|---|
| black today — first match wins | 98.52 % |
| `from_lines(chain(...))` union | **66.22 %** |
| deepest file with a matching pattern decides | 99.96 % |

The union loses ~1,670 queries. The shape I kept hitting is sideways leakage: `a/.gitignore: *.py`
starts ignoring `b/x.py`, because a pattern that was scoped to one subtree is now global.

**The prose in your recap *is* the fix.** "Apply per file, deepest consulted last" is git's rule, but
it's the layer black has to write — pathspec won't do it for you. In black's terms that's six lines,
precisely because the per-file specs already exist:

```diff
--- a/src/black/files.py
+++ b/src/black/files.py
@@ def _path_is_ignored(
     path = root / root_relative_path
-    # Note that this logic is sensitive to the ordering of gitignore_dict. Callers must
-    # ensure that gitignore_dict is ordered from least specific to most specific.
-    for gitignore_path, pattern in gitignore_dict.items():
+    # The deepest .gitignore with any matching pattern decides, as git does; shallower
+    # files are only consulted if no deeper one matched. Callers must ensure that
+    # gitignore_dict is ordered from least specific to most specific.
+    for gitignore_path, pattern in reversed(list(gitignore_dict.items())):
         try:
             relative_path = path.relative_to(gitignore_path).as_posix()
             if path.is_dir():
                 relative_path = relative_path + "/"
         except ValueError:
-            break
-        if pattern.match_file(relative_path):
-            return True
+            continue
+        result = pattern.check_file(relative_path)
+        if result.include is not None:
+            return result.include
     return False
```

`check_file` returns `include=None` when no pattern in that file matched, which is exactly "then ask
the file above". It exists in pathspec 1.0.0, the minimum black already requires — `pathspec>=1.0.0`
is a direct runtime dependency in `pyproject.toml`, not a transitive dev one, and black already
imports `GitIgnoreSpec` from it.

On 16 hand-built fixtures: black today 13/16, the union 13/16, this 16/16. On black's own gitignore
fixtures the collected file lists are byte-identical before and after — I rebuilt
`nested_gitignore_tests`, `ignore_subfolders_gitignore_tests` and `ignore_directory_gitignore_tests`
from `main` and diffed the sources both ways. I have **not** run black's test suite; black isn't
installed on the machine I measured this on, and I'd rather say so than imply coverage I don't have.

Two loose ends, in the interest of not overselling this:

- The residual 2 of 4,938 above is a single shape, and it is not the combination rule. Root
  `.gitignore` with `b/` then `!c/`, path `c/b/keep.py`: git ignores it (`b/` decides at `c/b`), while
  pathspec's `!c/` also matches everything *under* `c`, so the negation wins on index. That's a
  pathspec-level detail, same neighbourhood as cpburnz/python-pathspec#134.
- Your second suggested regression test asserts the opposite of git. Root excluding `packages/` with
  `packages/.gitignore: !packages/keep.py` — and also the charitable reading, `!keep.py` — leaves
  `packages/keep.py` **ignored** in git, both ways. It is not possible to re-include a file whose
  parent directory is excluded; that's in gitignore(5), and it's why the fix has to keep the directory
  pruning rather than drop it. Landing that test would freeze in the wrong behaviour.

And a correction to my own issue text while I'm here: I wrote that this is "more than a four-line
change". Having actually measured it, it's a six-line change to `_path_is_ignored`, because black
already keeps the per-file specs. The offer stands and it's a smaller PR than I made it sound — say
the word and I'll open it against `main` with the repro as a regression test and the fuzz harness in
the description.

— Midas

issues.title: potential multiprocessing performance improvement
issues.body:
I swear this isn't just an advertisement for my youtube video... but along the same lines of my youtube video [multiprocessing: slow things first](https://youtu.be/h4vmU2DJoQg) I believe there's some optimization potential to the scheduling of files for black

I initially thought about this a bit when receiving a report from [freecad](https://github.com/freecad/freecad) about slow execution of black in pre-commit.ci -- (sorta unrelated to this) after looking into it I noticed two significant improvements to their setup: (1) use the pre-compiled black (next pre-commit.ci autoupdate will do this fleetwide automatically!) and (2) there were a bunch of very large files which black was spending most of its time on 

the second is interesting to me and where I reminded myself of potential optimizations!  the tl;dr of the optimization is to attempt "slower" things first such that a scheduler can appropriately binpack smaller things later (imagine the worst case scenario where the last thing you schedule is the slowest one and you've significantly extended your execution time while having mostly idle cores)

I decided to try an experiment with black and see if applying a similar optimization could improve performance.  my numbers below are on a VM with 12 cores against [this version of freecad](https://github.com/freecad/freecad/commit/bae76a4dc0a0cca79a55eec5b093258e34b95ba1) with this diff applied:

```diff
diff --git a/.pre-commit-config.yaml b/.pre-commit-config.yaml
index 101f719e..8e277c8d 100644
--- a/.pre-commit-config.yaml
+++ b/.pre-commit-config.yaml
@@ -44,7 +44,6 @@ exclude: |
         src/Gui/3Dconnexion/navlib|
         src/Gui/QSint|
         src/Gui/Quarter|
-        src/Mod/Fem/femexamples|
         src/Mod/Import/App/SCL|
         src/Mod/Import/App/SCL_output|
         src/Mod/Mesh/App/TestData|
@@ -70,3 +69,13 @@ repos:
     rev: 719856d56a62953b8d2839fb9e851f25c3cfeef8  # frozen: v21.1.2
     hooks:
         -   id: clang-format
+-   repo: local
+    hooks:
+    - id: black-local
+      name: black
+      description: "Black: The uncompromising Python code formatter"
+      entry: black --line-length 100
+      language: system
+      minimum_pre_commit_version: 2.9.2
+      require_serial: true
+      types_or: [python, pyi]
```

and I wrote a little shell script to run this:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euxo pipefail

pip uninstall -yqq black
pip install -qq /tmp/black --no-deps

rm -rf ~/.cache/black
pre-commit run black-local --all-files --verbose
```

(note this uses non-precompiled black -- I suspect the numbers are similar but maybe a little less pronounced on a precompiled black)

(note also I haven't intentionally chosen a terrible set of files -- if I wanted a worst case scenario I'd probably delete every file after the ones in `src/Mod/Fem/femexamples` such that it schedules those last)

first a little baseline -- I ran this a few times and this particular run seemed representative (again, not very scientific performance benchmark but I was mostly just exploring the idea)

```console
$ bash t.sh 
+ pip uninstall -yqq black
+ pip install -qq /tmp/black --no-deps
+ rm -rf /home/asottile/.cache/black
+ pre-commit run black-local --all-files --verbose
black....................................................................Passed
- hook id: black-local
- duration: 32.82s

All done! ✨ 🍰 ✨
1002 files left unchanged.

```

after applying this patch to black (which naively assumes that larger files will be slower -- I think this is a pretty good assumption):

```diff
diff --git a/src/black/concurrency.py b/src/black/concurrency.py
index f6a2b8a..fd8db5f 100644
--- a/src/black/concurrency.py
+++ b/src/black/concurrency.py
@@ -164,7 +164,7 @@ async def schedule_formatting(
                 executor, format_file_in_place, src, fast, mode, write_back, lock
             )
         ): src
-        for src in sorted(sources)
+        for src in sorted(sources, key=lambda f: (-f.stat().st_size, f))
     }
     pending = tasks.keys()
     try:
```

I get a pretty significant improvement! (again: anecdotal -- though a few runs were similar in timing)

```console
$ bash t.sh 
+ pip uninstall -yqq black
+ pip install -qq /tmp/black --no-deps
+ rm -rf /home/asottile/.cache/black
+ pre-commit run black-local --all-files --verbose
```

issues.title: Preserve alignment of inline comments
issues.body:
**Describe the style change**

If inline comments have been aligned, that has most likely been done for a reason and breaking the alignment is likely to make the code worse. As an example, we have this code in our project:
```python
TypeHint = Union[
    type,                     # Actual type.
    str,                      # Type name or alias.
    UnionType,                # Union syntax (e.g. `int | float`).
    'tuple[TypeHint, ...]'    # Tuple of type hints. Behaves like a union.
]
```

**Examples in the current _Black_ style**

Currently the above example is formatted like this:

```python
TypeHint = Union[
    type,  # Actual type.
    str,  # Type name or alias.
    UnionType,  # Union syntax (e.g. `int | float`).
    'tuple[TypeHint, ...]',  # Tuple of type hints. Behaves like a union.
]
```

**Desired style**

I'd prefer the original formatting of comments to be preserved. Well, I would be fine if there would be just two spaces between the longest item and its comment instead of the current four.

**Additional context**

The situation changes if the code itself needs to be formatted or if inline comments are so long that they violate the max line length. Neither of these are true in our case and, in my opinion, the formatted code is clearly worse than the original.

I also ran into this issue in our project where we use aligned inline comments to document dictionary fields and type hints. The current Black behavior of normalizing all trailing comments to two spaces removes meaningful visual structure that was deliberately placed there.

**Before Black formatting (original, readable):**
```python
TypeHint = Union[
    type,                   # Actual type.
    str,                    # Type name or alias.
    uniontype,              # Union syntax (e.g. 'int | float').
    'Tuple[TypeHint, ...]'  # Tuple of type hints. Behaves like a union.
```

**After Black formatting (alignment lost):**
```python
TypeHint = Union[
    type,  # Actual type.
    str,  # Type name or alias.
    uniontype,  # Union syntax (e.g. 'int | float').
    'Tuple[TypeHint, ...]',  # Tuple of type hints. Behaves like a union.
]
```

As a workaround, we are currently using `# fmt: off` / `# fmt: on` blocks:

```python
# fmt: off

    type,                   # Actual type.
    str,                    # Type name or alias.
    uniontype,              # Union syntax (e.g. 'int | float').
    'Tuple[TypeHint, ...]'  # Tuple of type hints. Behaves like a union.
]
# fmt: on
```

This works but disables **all** Black formatting within that block, which is not ideal.

I think Black could at least **preserve existing alignment** when:
1. The comments are already aligned by the developer.
2. No line exceeds the configured max line length.

This would be a non-breaking improvement. Would love to see this addressed. Happy to help test or provide more real-world examples if useful.

## Describe the style change

When a "dot-chain" extends over the line length, black does different line breaks depending on a number of parameters that I don't fully understand, but I think include e.g.

- Whether elements of the chain have brackets (i.e. We are choosing an element from a list or a map)
- Whether the chain is standalone, or a function argument.
- Possibly the target python version

Simply breaking before or after the dot seems very sensible, but black sometimes does this, sometimes not, even if the line length limit is broken. Beyond that, breaking inside the brackets can make sense, but only if other reasons dictate it. I don't know whether all of this is by design or not, just bringing it up in case it can be changed and improved. issues.title: Test organization improvements
issues.body:
Part of #2238
While working on my first PR to the repo, I've noticed that interacting with the test cases is not easy.
This is because of how much is in each file, with the longest being ~1200 lines long. Because it's a test that uses `# output`, the input and output for a specific case are ~600 lines apart. This is made worse by the fact that formatting changes line counts, so getting back to the source isn't as easy as dividing the line number by 2. Running the test case also doesn't help, as it only reports the end failure, and nothing about the original input.

With the current framework, the way I can see to solve this would be splitting cases into their own files, inside folders. For example, instead of one big `preview_long_strings__regression.py` file, there would be a `preview_long_strings__regression` folder with contents named `preview_long_strings__regression_1.py`, `preview_long_strings__regression_2.py`, etc.

This would be really nice for making all the tests more local, as if a set of tests fails, each one would have it's input directly next to it's output, and each test case would be individually re-runnable with pytest.

I'm not sure how this would affect the performance, since I don't know the cost of running a bunch of tiny files vs one large file.

I'm not sure if the current test runner supports running cases inside folders, but given the current structure I assume so.

If for whatever reason a test ever needed to be removed, this would make it a different type of difficult, as instead of having to find the input in a long file, now all test files after the one being removed would have to be renamed.

If this is a thing that is wanted, I'd be happy to start work on the PR.

What you describe isn't actually Black's current style.

issues.title: Option to force "chop down" multiline (+ add magic comma) when line too long
issues.body:
I'd say that this is somewhere between a bug report and a feature request. Consider the following piece of code:

```python
def really_really_really_long_function_name(with_long_arguments, that_would_fit_on, one_line):
    another_really_really_long_function_name(with_long_arguments, that_would_fit_on, one_line)

    a_really_really_really_really_long_list = [with_long_arguments, that_would_fit_on, one_line]
    
    a_really_really_really_really_long_set = {with_long_arguments, that_would_fit_on, one_line}

    a_really_really_really_really_long_tuple = (with_long_arguments, that_would_fit_on, one_line)

    a_really_really_really_really_long_dict = {"a": with_long_arguments, "b": that_would_fit_on, "c": one_line}
```

Currently, black formats it as:

```python
def really_really_really_long_function_name(
    with_long_arguments, that_would_fit_on, one_line
):
    another_really_really_long_function_name(
        with_long_arguments, that_would_fit_on, one_line
    )

    a_really_really_really_really_long_list = [
        with_long_arguments,
        that_would_fit_on,
        one_line,
    ]

    a_really_really_really_really_long_set = {
        with_long_arguments,
        that_would_fit_on,
        one_line,
    }

    a_really_really_really_really_long_tuple = (
        with_long_arguments,
        that_would_fit_on,
        one_line,
    )

    a_really_really_really_really_long_dict = {
        "a": with_long_arguments,
        "b": that_would_fit_on,
        "c": one_line,
    }
```

which is inconsistent between function calls/definitions and list/set/tuple/dict literals.

I know, that you can force that same "long" multiline syntax by adding a magic comma after the last parameter/argument, however that requires manual intervention and (imho) doesn't fit into the normally opinionated black semantics.

I understand that some people might prefer this behaviour, but I often use black to format old, poorly formatted codebases and in those cases I almost **never** want this "intermediate" multiline style. IMHO, either the arguments should be refactored so that they fit on the same line as the function name, or they should be "properly" split over multiple lines:
```python
def really_really_really_long_function_name(
    with_long_arguments,
    that_would_fit_on,
    one_line,
):
    another_really_really_long_function_name(
        with_long_arguments,
        that_would_fit_on,
        one_line,
    )
```

I would like to request an option `--force-magic-trailing-comma` or `--insert-magic-trailing-comma` (name open to bike shedding) that would automatically add a trailing comma when black is forced to wrap parameter/argument lists and split them into proper "one argument per line" multilines.

issues.title: Future of `string_processing`
issues.body:
We merged string processing in May 2020 (#1132), almost four years ago. A few months later, I put the feature behind a flag because there were too many related bugs (#1609). Four years later, we're still in basically the same state: most of the open issues in https://github.com/psf/black/labels/C%3A%20preview%20style are about string processing.

I'm also increasingly convinced that string_processing's core feature, splitting up long strings, would be exceedingly controversial if we ever did turn it on by default. It is just too hard for a tool to figure out how to split a string in a way that makes sense to readers of the code. However, there are other things that string_processing does, and some of those are valuable and could perhaps be split off.

So my proposal is:
- Give up on splitting strings automatically; Black will simply not do that
- Split out any other useful features from string-processing into separate preview features that we can reasonably hope to enable in next year's stable style.

If you're interested in getting any part of string_processing into stable Black, please contribute a PR moving it to a separate preview feature.

I ran string_processing on my work codebase and noticed a few specific changes that could be split out. I'll list them in a separate comment.

issues.title: Enable enable-unstable-feature = ['string_processing'] without preview flag
issues.body:
<!--
Please make sure that the bug is not already fixed either in newer versions or the
current development version. To confirm this, you have three options:

1. Update Black's version if a newer release exists: `pip install -U black`
2. Use the online formatter at <https://black.vercel.app/?version=main>, which will use
   the latest main branch.
3. Or run _Black_ on your machine:
   - create a new virtualenv (make sure it's the same Python version);
   - clone this repository;
   - run `pip install -e .[d]`;
   - run `pip install -r test_requirements.txt`
   - make sure it's sane by running `python -m pytest`; and
   - run `black` like you did last time.
-->

**Describe the bug**
In 2023 we used experimental-string-processing. This was enabled without preview style enabled.
However now in 2024 the experimental string processing flag was removed and replaced with
enable-unstable-feature = ['string_processing']

However this feature requires turning on the preview feature.
And now the files are additionally formated based on the preview style.

**To Reproduce**

```
preview = true
enable-unstable-feature = ['string_processing']
skip-string-normalization = true
```
vs:
```
experimental-string-processing = true
skip-string-normalization = true
```

We would like to go according to official style but have better string processing enabled. Without that we get bunch of line too long errors in the code.

For example, take this code (first without preview and the second with):
![image](https://github.com/psf/black/assets/3091122/6e60e4d7-6ced-46d9-8a63-153837ea4319)

**Expected behavior**
I like that you are formalizing the enable-unstable-feature in such way but not that it requires preview with additional modifications. So unstable processing without other preview style (like in 2023).

**Environment**

<!-- Please complete the following information: -->

- Black's version: 24.1.1
- OS and Python version: Python 3.11.0

comments.author: hauntsaninja
comments.body:
Thanks for the issue! This was intentional. Our goal with `--enable-unstable-feature` was not to let users pick and choose parts of Black's future style (Black will simply never be configurable in that kind of way). It was to give Black a way to develop risky or problematic changes, while allowing us to potentially gain feedback and to allow users of such features a way to avoid thrash in their code in the event we mark a preview feature as unstable. See https://github.com/psf/black/issues/4093 for more.

With that said, I'm sympathetic to the fact that despite being explicitly experimental `--experimental-string-processing` has a long history, and that this is a regression in the utility Black provides you. I'm still inclined to not make a change here, but I'm potentially willing to reconsider if it turns out that there are a lot of people eager to regain `--experimental-string-processing` but unwilling to use `--preview`. And of course, other maintainers may have other opinions.

comments.author: matejsp
comments.body:
IMHO Best way forward would be to make experimental string processing non experimental :D
The default config just doesn't work. One thing would be to leave correctly formated string but black just corrupts it (we get hundreds of line too longs warnings).

We have been using it for past year (on around 500k LOC) and it work without a problem (compatible with ruff, flake8, pylint). Without having (only) experimental processing latest black has became a bit useless for us :(

Also on larger code base it would be benefical to enable just some parts of preview features (in case they can be applied in isolation). It would be easier to test and not introduce too many changes in the code. The preview functionality gets in the end cherry picked anyway making it even better argument for such isolated preview features. Why not allow us to do the same during the development for next year style and be more engaged in the future black style :)

comments.author: JelleZijlstra
comments.body:
> One thing would be to leave correctly formated string but black just corrupts it (we get hundreds of line too longs warnings).

Could you provide more detail on this? It sounds like a bug and I don't think that's Black's normal behavior.

```
% cat longstring.py 
x = "a b c d d e f g h i j k l m n o p q r s t u v w x y z a b c d e f g h i j k l m n o p q r s t u v w x y z a b c d e f g h i j k l m n o p q r s t u v w x y z"
% black --unstable longstring.py 
reformatted longstring.py

All done! ✨ 🍰 ✨
1 file reformatted.
% cat longstring.py 
x = (
    "a b c d d e f g h i j k l m n o p q r s t u v w x y z a b c d e f g h i j k l m n"
    " o p q r s t u v w x y z a b c d e f g h i j k l m n o p q r s t u v w x y z"
)
% black longstring.py 
All done! ✨ 🍰 ✨
1 file left unchanged.
% cat longstring.py  
x = (
    "a b c d d e f g h i j k l m n o p q r s t u v w x y z a b c d e f g h i j k l m n"
    " o p q r s t u v w x y z a b c d e f g h i j k l m n o p q r s t u v w x y z"
)
```

> The preview functionality gets in the end cherry picked anyway making it even better argument for such isolated preview features.

This is why we added the new `--unstable` style this year: we noticed that we often skipped out large parts of the preview style at the end of the year, making `--preview` not very useful as a preview of next year's style. This year, we put features we wouldn't currently stabilize in `--unstable` alone, so that `--preview` is much more likely to match next year's stable style.

> IMHO Best way forward would be to make experimental string processing non experimental :D

If you want this to happen, there's a long list of issues related to it listed in #4042 that need to be fixed.
